takeaway: MigrRDMA pre-establishes replacement RDMA resources, virtualizes exposed identifiers, and drains in-flight requests so containers can migrate across commodity Mellanox RNICs without hardware changes.
background: Live migration normally copies memory while a service keeps running, then briefly stops it to transfer the remaining state. RDMA complicates this because applications directly observe RNIC-managed queue and memory-region identifiers, while in-flight work requests and completion entries live across software and hardware.
villain: Recreating every RDMA resource only after stop-and-copy lengthens blackout, but recreating resources early changes identifiers and memory mappings. Simply stopping the process can also lose, duplicate, or reorder in-flight RDMA work, and hardware-assisted proposals require modified RNICs.
approach: MigrRDMA extends Mellanox OFED, CRIU, and runc. During memory pre-copy it maps RDMA-related structures at their original virtual addresses and creates replacement resources and connections at the destination. A driver/library indirection layer translates virtual QP and memory keys to the old or new physical identifiers. Before stop-and-copy, the migrated endpoint and every communication partner suspend new work, drain in-flight work requests, retain unconsumed completions in fake queues, and replay buffered work after restoration.
impact: The authors show that software coordination can preserve application-visible RDMA state and shorten migration blackout on unmodified commodity RNICs, including for an unmodified RDMA-based Hadoop binary.

evaluation.overview: The evaluation decomposes migration blackout, checks work-request and completion consistency, measures wait-before-stop and virtualization costs, follows throughput during migration, and migrates RDMA-based Hadoop.
evaluation.implemented: A container-migration prototype based on Mellanox OFED 5.4, with about 4,500 C lines in the kernel driver, 11,000 in the userspace RDMA library, 3,200 in CRIU, and 1,100 in runc; Docker and application binaries are unchanged.
evaluation.setting: The six-server testbed has one source, one destination, and four communication partners connected by one Arista 7260CX3-64 switch. Every server has dual 16-core Intel Xeon E5-2698 v3 CPUs, 256 GB RAM, and a ConnectX-5 100 Gb/s RNIC. Perftest exercises SEND/RECV/READ/WRITE patterns; the application experiment uses one HDFS master and two slave containers.
baselines: The same software migration workflow without RDMA pre-setup
The same RDMA operations without identifier virtualization

results.text: Across migrated-sender and migrated-receiver WRITE and SEND/RECV microbenchmarks with 1–4,096 QPs, pre-establishing RDMA resources reduced blackout by up to 58% relative to the same workflow that restored RDMA only after stop-and-copy.

For one reliable-connected QP sending 64-byte messages for five seconds, identifier virtualization added 4.6–8.3 CPU cycles per SEND, RECV, WRITE, or READ operation, corresponding to 3.7%–8.9% overhead after excluding busy-poll cycles.

limitations: Wait-before-stop requires the migrated service and all of its communication partners to run MigrRDMA; a regular-RDMA partner cannot participate in migration, and mixed deployments exclude one-sided virtualization unless they add special negotiation. Partners must have enough spare QPs for replacement connections. The experiments use one switch and ConnectX-5 RNICs, and the MigrOS comparison is theoretical because its published prototype uses SoftRoCE rather than hardware. A timeout handles spotty networks by replaying unfinished work, so the normal drain-before-stop argument depends on communication completing before that timeout.
phd_group_signal: This is systems work at the OS/network boundary: identify externally visible device state, introduce the smallest indirection needed to relocate it, coordinate distributed endpoints around a cutover, and validate both correctness and data-path overhead.
beginner_concepts: RDMA queue pairs and work requests

claims.text: MigrRDMA restores RDMA-related memory and creates destination resources during pre-copy, translates virtual QPNs and access keys in the software driver/library path, and uses coordinated wait-before-stop plus fake completion queues and replay to preserve in-flight and unconsumed work.

The migration protocol assumes software support at every communication partner and spare partner-side queue pairs; services with a non-MigrRDMA partner cannot be migrated, and mixed-environment one-sided operations require additional handling because virtual-to-physical remote-key mappings cannot otherwise be exchanged.
